results.title: Google TurboQuant — Paper, Tools, Benchmarks & Framework Status
results.content:
## When TurboQuant matters most

1

### Long-context serving

RAG pipelines, document Q&A, and multi-turn chat at 32k–128k tokens per request. KV cache is the dominant memory cost at these lengths.

2

### Batch inference at scale

Serving multiple concurrent requests where KV cache memory limits batch size. Reducing cache per request means more concurrent users per GPU.

3

### Consumer GPU deployment [...] Decoder models cache attention keys and values so they do not recompute the full prefix at every step. As context grows, this cache dominates GPU memory — often more than the model weights themselves at 128k+ contexts.

KV cache memory formula

2 × kv\_heads × head\_dim × layers × context\_len × batch × bytes

A single Llama 3.1 70B request at 128k context in FP16 needs an estimated ~40 GB just for KV cache (based on the KV formula). At a 3-bit target, TurboQuant would reduce that to ~7.5 GB. [...] ### Paper claims

Google reports at least 6× KV memory reduction, near-lossless 3-bit quantization on tested benchmarks, and up to 8× faster attention on H100.

D

### Deployment questions

Your outcome depends on model architecture (MHA, GQA, MQA), context length, batch size, and the rest of your inference stack.

## Why KV cache is the real bottleneck

results.title: TurboQuant: Google Just Solved the KV Cache Bottleneck
results.content:
I ran this for five pairs with 3000 independent quantizations each, measuring the t-statistic (a standard test for whether a mean differs from zero; |t| < 2 means no detectable bias):

```
TQ_MSE t-stats: [25.5, 23.0, 26.5, 34.9, 24.8] → clearly biased (expected) TQ_Prod t-stats: [ 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 1.0, 0.8] → undetectable bias ✓ 
``` [...] arXiv:2504.19874. Reproduced for educational purposes. [...] This is the bottleneck. Not the weights — those are shared. The KV cache is private to each conversation, grows with every word, and cannot be compressed the way weights can. Weight quantization happens once offline. The KV cache is written token-by-token in real time. You compress each vector the moment it arrives, before knowing what the next token will be.

results.title: TurboQuant: What Developers Need to Know About ...
results.content:
The issue is simple: it grows linearly with context length, and it stores everything in full precision (typically FP16). For an 8B parameter model at 32K context, the KV cache alone can consume around 4.6 GB of VRAM. Scale that to multiple concurrent users or longer contexts, and you're out of memory before the model weights themselves become the bottleneck. [...] Short contexts don't benefit much. Below 1K tokens, the KV cache is small enough that compression savings are negligible and the overhead of rotation + quantization can even be a net negative. TurboQuant really shines at 4K+ tokens.

The residual window matters. Most implementations keep the most recent 128-256 tokens in full FP16 precision and only compress older tokens. This is important for output quality since attention focuses heavily on recent context. [...] Published by Google Research on March 24, 2026 and headed to ICLR 2026, TurboQuant is a compression algorithm that shrinks the KV cache -- the biggest memory bottleneck during LLM inference -- down to 3-4 bits per element without any retraining or fine-tuning. The result is roughly a 4-6x reduction in KV cache memory with negligible quality loss.

results.title: KV Cache Is Eating Your VRAM. Here's How Google Fixed ...
results.content: Though KV cache came as a silver lining for LLMs, it brought up more challenges. It introduced additional memory overhead. This might not be a big issue for SLMs, but mega-LLMs with billions of parameters now became more difficult to load on machines. Roughly 20-30% additional VRAM is consumed by the KV cache alone. results.title: What Is Google TurboQuant? The KV Cache Compression ...
results.content:
Per-head calibration. Rather than applying a single global quantization scheme across the entire KV cache, TurboQuant calibrates quantization parameters independently for each attention head. Different heads have different value distributions, and treating them uniformly wastes precision where it matters. [...] Google’s research claims accuracy that is statistically indistinguishable from full-precision KV cache on standard benchmarks, including long-context tasks. However, “zero accuracy loss” in this context means performance within the margin of error on the specific benchmarks tested, not a mathematical guarantee. Results may vary slightly depending on the task, model size, and context type. Independent replication of the benchmarks is still in early stages. [...] Before TurboQuant, most production systems stored KV cache in 16-bit (FP16 or BF16). Some aggressive deployments used 8-bit (INT8). Getting to 3 bits with no meaningful accuracy loss is a significant jump.

To put it concretely:

   A KV cache that previously required 60GB of GPU memory could be compressed to roughly 11GB.
   A single H100 with 80GB HBM could serve contexts or batch sizes that previously required multiple GPUs.
   Serving costs per token drop substantially.
